lines.text: In World War Two, a scientist trained pigeons to steer a bomb, and in the tests, it actually worked.
You see, in 1940, the psychologist B. F. Skinner was on a train, watching a flock of birds fly beside his window.
Sharp eyes, quick turns. Could birds like that guide a missile?
So he taught pigeons to peck at a picture of a target, for a grain of food.
One bird pecked over ten thousand times in forty-five minutes.
Then he put three of them in the nose of a glide bomb called the Pelican.
A lens showed them the view ahead. When the target drifted off center, their pecking steered the bomb back.
Three birds meant a vote. If one got it wrong, the other two outvoted it.
The government thought it was eccentric and impractical, but still paid twenty-five thousand dollars.
Then came the big demonstration. A live pigeon did its job perfectly, right in front of the committee.
Skinner wrote that seeing a real pigeon do it only reminded them how crazy the idea sounded.
The project was dropped. The Navy revived it in 1948, and tested pigeons until 1953.
Then, in 2024, the pigeon bomb finally won a prize. The Ig Nobel Peace Prize.
So the pigeons were never the problem. Nobody could take them seriously.
